title: Evolution & Biodiversity Adventure 2: Classification, cladistics and phylogeny
welcome_lead: Today you'll branch the tree of life — cladistics and the three domains.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Carl Linnaeus (1758) ranked life into nested groups:

Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

Binomial: Panthera leo. Mnemonic: 'Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.

Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters (synapomorphies), not overall similarity.

A clade = common ancestor + all descendants. Birds belong to clade Reptilia (sharing scales, amniotic egg with crocs).

Molecular phylogenetics uses sequence differences as a molecular clock.

Carl Woese (1977) used 16S rRNA to discover Archaea are distinct from Bacteria. Result: three domains replaced two empires.

- Bacteria — peptidoglycan walls.
- Archaea — extremophiles, ether-linked lipids.
- Eukarya — true nuclei.

This is a major paradigm shift — nature of science: molecular data overturned morphology-based classification.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct binomial for humans?
Which three domains classify all life?
How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.
Insulin works on muscles and glucagon works on the brain.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.

mcqs.q: How does ADH affect the collecting duct in the kidney?
options: Insulin works on muscles and glucagon works on the brain.
It increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water (by inserting aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and urine is more concentrated.
ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
ADH actively pumps water out of urine into the blood.

mcqs.q: How do insulin and glucagon work together to regulate blood glucose?
options: Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Insulin works on muscles and glucagon works on the brain.
Insulin and glucagon both lower blood glucose using different mechanisms.
They are antagonistic — insulin lowers blood glucose (cells take up glucose, store as glycogen); glucagon raises it (glycogen broken back down to glucose).
